Social engineering / phishing
Manipulates a person into revealing information or taking an unsafe action; phishing uses deceptive messages or sites.
Fake equipment-desk sign-in request.
Independent verification, reporting practice and MFA; training alone does not eliminate deception.
Denial of service
Exhausts or disrupts resources so legitimate users cannot use a service; distributed DoS involves multiple sources.
Loan portal overwhelmed by requests.
Traffic filtering/rate limits and provider support; ordinary backups do not keep the live service reachable.
Back door
A concealed or unintended route that bypasses normal access controls.
Undocumented maintenance account bypasses normal login.
Remove unnecessary access paths, review accounts/configuration and monitor use.
IP spoofing
Falsifies a packet’s source IP address; this does not prove the sender can receive replies or has authenticated.
Traffic claims to come from a trusted address.
Use authenticated communication and appropriate ingress/egress filtering; do not treat an IP address alone as identity.
SQL injection
Untrusted input is treated as SQL structure by an application.
A search form builds a query by concatenating input.
Parameterised statements and least database privilege; field validation is an additional check.
Man-in-the-middle
An intermediary intercepts and may alter communication between parties.
A false network intermediary relays portal traffic.
Authenticated encrypted connections, verified endpoints and certificate checks.
Cross-site scripting (XSS)
Untrusted content becomes executable script in a user’s browser through a vulnerable application.
A portal displays submitted notes as active page content.
Context-appropriate output encoding, safe DOM/template practices and sanitisation where HTML is allowed. SQL parameters do not prevent browser script execution.
Virus
Malicious code attaches to a host such as a file/program and spreads when the host executes.
Infected program copied between desk devices.
Trusted software, updates and endpoint protection.
Worm
Malware that can propagate between systems without attaching to a host file.
Malware spreads between vulnerable devices.
Patching, segmentation and endpoint protection.
Trojan horse
Malicious software disguised as a useful or legitimate program; the label describes deception, not self-replication.
Fake inventory utility installs unwanted code.
Approved software sources, application controls and limited privilege.
Spyware
Covertly collects information or monitors activity.
Software records desk activity or credentials.
Endpoint protection, permissions review and trusted software.
Adware
Software that displays advertising; unwanted or malicious variants can track users or disrupt work.
Unwanted advertising bundled with a utility.
Review installations, permissions and trusted sources; not every advertising-supported application is malware.
Ransomware
Malware that blocks access, often by encrypting data, and demands payment; attacks may also steal data.
Loan database becomes unreadable and an extortion message appears.
Prevention controls plus protected, tested backups and an incident plan; restoring data does not undo a disclosure.
Physical security threat
Physical access, theft, damage or environmental disruption can compromise a system.
Unlocked desk laptop is stolen; a power loss interrupts service.
Restricted access, locked storage, screen locks, suitable power protection and recovery arrangements.
Zero-day vulnerability
A previously unknown vulnerability may be exploited before defenders have a practical fix. It is a weakness, not a malware category.
A newly disclosed application flaw has no patch available yet.
Reduce exposure, use temporary mitigations and monitoring, then apply a verified fix when available.
